chapters.name: Technology
chapters.descriptionLong: The technology leaderboards have been constant feature in our Developer Surveys from the beginning. That’s the core of the software developer’s toolkit; what’s changed are the categories of tech on this list. Cloud providers, coding agents, LLMs, and security ops.  Many of the top technologies in some of these lists have been there for years. Some lists show clear leaders in the space. But every one of these lists show that there is plenty of room for alternative technologies, as each of these lists has a large number of technologies in the single digits for usage (and we had to cut off the lists at some point).

features.headline: The Core Stack: Technologies that stand the test of time
features.description:
The majority of developers are using JavaScript, SQL, HTML/CSS, Python, and Bash/Shell. Not too surprising; these are the basic techs involved in web software, and everything is web software these days. No real complaints here, about a third of folks want to use these techs in 6 months (except for the shell languages (25%) and HTML (29%) because can’t we get a script to write that?). AI seems to love using JavScript and Python (38% each).

For the backend (and standalone) languages, things get a little more diversified. Java and C# both top here, ~27%, though C# seems to leave a slightly better impression, as slightly more people want to use it in the next six months. Rust perennially has more admirers than users. Other languages more admired than used include Zig, Haskel, Elixir, and Erlang.
Postgres continues reign as the most used database, used by a majority of respondents.

Postgres continues to rule in the database space. In an interview on [Stack Overflow’s podcast Shireesh Thota](https://stackoverflow.blog/2026/02/17/data-is-the-new-oil/) (Corporate VP of Azure Databases at Microsoft) said "I tell everyone that Postgres is the Linux of databases... It's one of the best open source projects out there where the community really rallies. They care deeply."  Is it also the AI gateway drug?  That’s how Brian O'Grady (Head of Field Research at Qdrant) put it when he summarized in a [separate interview](https://stackoverflow.blog/2026/05/05/what-un-exactly-do-you-mean-by-semantic-search/) with us the ease of starting with its vector capabilities: "I've called it almost like a gateway drug to vector search. As soon as you use pgvector, you're in."

features.headline: I tell everyone that Postgres is the Linux of databases... It's one of the best open source projects out there where the community really rallies. They care deeply.
features.description: Shireesh Thota, Corporate VP of Azure Databases at Microsoft ([source](https://stackoverflow.blog/2026/02/17/data-is-the-new-oil/))

features.headline: Builders are still building in the age of AI
features.description: When developers open their IDEs to build in-house software, popular predictions of an AI-driven "SaaSpocalypse" turn out to be greatly exaggerated. Developers are building at high volumes, but their focus remains heavily on internal utilities and glue code rather than replacing commercial software. 77% of developers build small scripts and automations, while 63% create team-level internal tools.  54% build customer-facing applications—a reminder that a vast portion of engineers work inside traditional enterprise sectors like retail, finance, and manufacturing. Vendor replacement sits at the bottom: Only 16% of respondents build in-house software to replace paid vendors.
Small scripts are most common for builders to work on, 19% say they’re building tools to replace paid vendors.

When cross-referencing these builds with AI tool usage, a subtle trend emerges: AI adoption steadily drops as system complexity and operational risk increase. While 54% of developers replacing vendors utilize AI assistance, this represents a rate only within that specific subgroup. Across the entire survey pool, just 10% of total developers are using AI to replace third-party software. Far from being an AI break-out story, vendor replacement is actually the workload where AI assistance hits its lowest penetration ceiling. The survey's AI friction data explains why developers hesitate to replace SaaS vendors with custom LLM-generated software. Paid tools offload security compliance, SLAs, and continuous maintenance. Replacing them transfers technical debt back onto internal teams, right where AI errors create the most pain. Developers are happy to let AI generate low-risk automation scripts, but when it comes to business-critical SaaS, most teams still prefer paying a vendor over managing unmaintainable, AI-generated technical debt.
While only 16% say they’re building tools to replace paid vendors, of that cohort more than half are doing so with the help of AI.

features.headline: Frontier models’ next evolution
features.description: While OpenAI and Anthropic sit neck-and-neck at the top of general LLM usage (74% and 75% adoption each), practitioner sentiment reveals a clear divergence when evaluating developer preference and agentic execution. Anthropic holds a sharp lead in forward-looking interest, with 49% of developers expressing a desire to work with Claude over the next six months, compared to 32% for OpenAI. When building autonomous coding agents or complex tool-calling pipelines, developers lean heavily toward Anthropic (45% usage) over OpenAI (32% usage). Spend tracking data from Ramp mirrors this shift, showing Anthropic capturing market share rapidly as engineering teams transition from simple chat interfaces to structured, programmatic agent architectures.
The two companies focused on frontier models are the top two in LLM usage: Anthropic at 75% and OpenAI at 74%.

Disruption and security still remain areas for improvement.  Many in the survey did not indicate working with security technology, showing us that AI security ops  is still more of an isolated field, possibly a good target for those looking to add future-forward tools into their regimen.  Without the security practitioners we see 23% of users indicate their team lost valuable time to security or privacy issues stemming from AI.
For all the talk of security work shifting left, only 23% of respondents have used security tools in the past year.
